opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly the line is blurrier than people think. The way I tend to frame it is: where does the cost of being wrong get really high, and where is the space of possible behaviors too large to cover by testing or intuition?

So if you think about something like an access control policy in the cloud, you might have a policy that's a few hundred lines long, with conditions on principals, resources, IP ranges, time of day, and so on. The number of possible requests that could be evaluated against that policy is effectively infinite. You can't test your way to confidence there. And the consequence of a mistake is that some data bucket is open to the world. That combination, an enormous state space plus a high cost of failure, is the signal that you want proof rather than sampling.

Contrast that with, say, picking a font for a webpage. Nobody needs a theorem about that. Even plenty of business logic falls into a middle ground where good engineering practice, code review and testing get you most of the way there.

But what's been interesting to me over the last decade or so is that once you start looking, you find a lot more of the first category than you expected. Cryptographic libraries, hypervisors, storage systems with durability guarantees, network reachability, authorization. Anything with "never" or "always" in its requirement. "Customer data is never accessible outside this account." "This write is always durable once acknowledged." Those universal statements are really the tell. Testing can show you the presence of bugs, as Dijkstra said, but it can't establish an "always."

And then there's a newer category, which is where generative AI comes in. When you have a model producing answers about, say, an HR policy or a tax rule or a mortgage eligibility rule, and someone is going to act on that answer, you've again got a situation where correctness really matters and the space of questions is unbounded. So there's a growing role for formalizing the underlying rules and checking the model's output against them, so you can say not just "this sounds right" but "this follows from the policy, and here's why."

So the practical heuristic I'd give people is: look for the universal claims you're implicitly making to customers, look at how big the input space is, and ask what it costs if you're wrong. Where all three are high, that's where formal reasoning pays for itself, and in my experience it's also where it ends up making teams move faster, not slower, because they stop being afraid to change the system.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that most of the time you don't need it. If I'm deciding where to go for lunch, I'm not going to write down a formal specification and prove a theorem about it. The cost of getting it wrong is low and the feedback loop is fast. I'll know in an hour whether I made a bad choice.

Where formal reasoning starts to earn its keep is when a few things line up. First, the consequences of being wrong are severe or hard to reverse. Security is the obvious example. If you mis-configure access to a storage bucket, you don't find out by having a bad lunch, you find out when your data is on the front page of a newspaper. Second, the space of possible behaviors is too large to test your way through. If a system has thousands of configuration options and they interact, you can run a million tests and still miss the one path that matters. Third, there's a precise question you can actually state. "Is this system good?" isn't a formal question. "Can any principal outside this account ever read this resource?" is. Once you can write the question down crisply, you've done most of the work, and then the automated tools can do the rest.

So in my own thinking I ask: how bad is failure, how big is the space I'd have to explore by hand, and can I state the property I care about unambiguously? If all three point the same direction, that's where I want a proof rather than a vibe. And I'd add that a lot of what looks like everyday reasoning at a place like Amazon actually turns out to be in that category once you look closely. Network reachability, IAM policies, cryptographic protocols. People used to treat those as judgment calls made by experienced engineers. They're really mathematical questions, and once you treat them that way you can answer them for every customer, every time, instead of relying on someone being careful on a Tuesday afternoon.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of the consequences of getting something wrong, and how hard it is to discover that you’ve got it wrong. If you’re choosing where to have lunch, you probably don’t need formal reasoning. You can try something, get feedback, and make a different choice next time. But if you’re deciding whether someone should have access to sensitive data, or whether a system can lose your data, then you’d like a stronger assurance.

The other consideration is the number of possibilities. A process can look quite simple and still have an enormous number of behaviors because of the ways its parts interact. Testing lets you examine particular cases. Formal reasoning lets you ask whether a property holds across every case covered by your model.

So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line between two kinds of processes. I’d ask: What’s the claim we need to establish? What would happen if it were false? And is testing enough to give us the confidence we need? Often, you only need formal reasoning for a small, critical part of a much larger process.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is less about whether a process needs formal reasoning in principle and more about what’s at stake if we get it wrong. If I’m deciding what to have for lunch, I’m quite happy with intuition. If I’m designing a system that controls access to sensitive data, I want a much stronger argument that it behaves correctly.

Testing gives you examples of what happens. Formal reasoning lets you ask, “For every possible input, and every possible sequence of events, does this property hold?” That becomes especially valuable when there are so many combinations that you couldn’t realistically test them all.

And it doesn’t have to be all or nothing. You can identify one particularly important property of a system and prove that, while using ordinary engineering techniques for the rest.
